lessons.title: Voice is not a closed box
lessons.why: The call is not finished when it rings. Recording, staffing, location, analytics, CRM, and agents are part of the same job.
body: Teams Phone gets a number to a person or a voice app. Around that call sit Cloud Voicemail, emergency location, a certified recorder, a queue’s interval stats, a CRM case, and sometimes a bot. Each of those is a sister system with its own configuration and its own failure.
This track is the map of those systems. It does not replace the earlier tracks. If the trunk is down, the CRM pop is not the lead.

flow.label: Sisters
flow.detail: Recording, WFM, E911, analytics, CRM, agent

chart.title: Sister systems
chart.note: They attach. They are not Teams Phone.

lessons.say: I can name the sister system and the identifier that joins it to the call.
lessons.fault: A CRM bug is debugged as an SBC outage, or the reverse.
lessons.listen: The ecosystem is everything attached to the call. Name the system, then the join key, then the fault.

lessons.title: How to use the glossary
lessons.why: The glossary is the shared language for the map. Interviews punish fuzzy words.
body: Each term has a plain definition, a reason it matters, a configuration hint, and a fault you should recognize. Filter by track. If a definition and a vendor blog disagree, open the source link. The access date is 14 October 2026.
Flashcards are the same facts in recall form. Do not treat a card you flipped once as evidence you can operate the system. The lab is that evidence.
lessons.say: I can define the term, the fault, and the document I would open.
lessons.fault: Two people use ‘recording’ and mean convenience and compliance.
lessons.listen: Use the glossary to keep words sharp. Recording, for example, is two different features.

lessons.title: The mind map
lessons.why: A picture of the estate stops you from buying a second phone system by accident.
body: The map puts Entra ID and Cloud Voicemail beside Teams Phone, the dial plan in front of routing, the SBC between Teams and the carrier, and emergency location on that SBC path. Attendants, Dynamics, ACS, Copilot Studio, recording, WFM, Power BI, and the CRM sit on named edges.

Click a node in the map view. The edge label is the thing that has to be true: user homed online, TLS 5061, a licensed resource account, a policy bot, queue intervals. If you cannot point at the edge, you do not understand the integration.
lessons.say: I can draw Teams, the SBC, the carrier, and the six sister systems without notes.
lessons.fault: A design has no picture, so recording and E911 are discovered after go-live.
lessons.listen: Use the mind map. Every edge is a requirement, not decoration.

lessons.title: Compliance recording and quality management
lessons.why: Regulated desks need a recorder the user cannot stop. Convenience recording is not that recorder.
body: Convenience recording is started by a licensed user and stored with the meeting. Compliance recording is a third-party bot invited by policy into new calls, meetings, and events. Microsoft’s comparison, accessed 14 October 2026, says notification is enforced, participant consent is not the compliance control, and audio-only is not the compliance mode. Listed media is voice, video, and screen share. Desktop screen recording, if you need the CRM window, is a separate product you must disclose.

Configuration: a certified recorder, an application instance, a policy created with New-CsTeamsComplianceRecordingPolicy and set enabled, the application attached, then Grant-CsTeamsComplianceRecordingPolicy to the users or groups. Granting the policy does not record if the instance is missing. Existing calls are unaffected. Test a new call. Retention lives in the partner system, not in meeting storage. Quality management scores those recordings with a form the agent has seen.

chart.title: Compliance gate
chart.note: All five, or it is not recording.

lessons.say: Compliance recording is a partner bot, a policy, and an application instance. Users do not start it. I test a new call.
lessons.fault: The policy is assigned and nothing records, because the bot instance was never created.
lessons.listen: Compliance recording needs a certified bot, an enabled policy, a grant, and a new test call. It is not the record button.

lessons.title: Workforce management
lessons.why: A queue without a staffing model is a guess. Teams user reports will not staff next Tuesday.
body: Workforce management consumes offered, answered, abandoned, and handle time from the contact center or the queue, in the same interval the schedule uses. Erlang C is a teaching model of how many people must be available. Shrinkage is the fraction of paid time that is not available. Roster is larger than the Erlang number. Occupancy is handle time over handle time plus ready time. Very high occupancy burns people and raises abandons.

Troubleshooting: if WFM says you were overstaffed while the queue overflowed, check whether overflow removed calls from this queue’s offered count, whether the interval was a day instead of 30 minutes, and whether handle time forgot after-call work. Agents set to available in Teams while still writing a case will poison both tools.

chart.title: Staffing stack
chart.note: Teaching relationship, not a vendor screen.

lessons.say: I staff from queue intervals, Erlang C, and an explicit shrinkage. I do not staff from Call Analytics.
lessons.fault: The forecast is ten times too high because the interval was a whole day.
lessons.listen: WFM eats queue intervals. Erlang C plus shrinkage is the teaching math. Do not feed it from a user’s call history.

lessons.title: E911 as a system of record
lessons.why: Location is data you operate, shared with routing and with quality maps.
body: Keep one subnet list. Emergency location, location-based routing, and the CQD building map should read it. Three spreadsheets will drift, and then E911 says London, CQD says VPN, and LBR says Manchester.

Configuration is the topology plus the emergency policy plus the route plus the carrier test. Troubleshooting starts with ‘which subnet did the client present,’ not with the SBC firmware. PIDF-LO only helps if the SBC and the carrier pass it on. Notification only helps if the policy is assigned.
lessons.say: One subnet list feeds emergency location, LBR, and CQD. I can say which consumer is wrong when they disagree.
lessons.fault: Three teams edit three maps and a VPN user inherits the HQ address.
lessons.listen: Treat emergency location as a system of record shared with LBR and CQD. One subnet list.

lessons.title: Analytics and Power BI
lessons.why: A dashboard is a view. Call Analytics, CQD, and contact-center analytics are different grains of truth.
body: Call Analytics is one call. CQD is the estate. Contact-center analytics are the queue: service level, abandon, handle time. Power BI can sit on CQD data, and contact-center implementations often surface supervisor numbers in Power BI. The report inherits a bad subnet map and a bad abandon rule.

Troubleshooting: if leadership sees a red headquarters, check the VPN labeling before you buy circuits. If two service-level numbers disagree, write down each abandon rule. Access to CQD is an admin permission. Do not share a password to get around that.

lessons.title: CRM and screen pop
lessons.why: The case is where the business remembers the call. Teams will not open Dynamics for an ordinary PSTN call by itself.
body: Screen pop is a contact-center or middleware behavior. It looks up a contact from the caller number. That number has to be E.164 after normalization. Store the SIP Call-ID, the queue, and the agent on the timeline. A note that says ‘called customer’ cannot be audited.

Troubleshooting: the wrong contact pops when a trunk prefix is still on the number, or when one human has two caller IDs. Teams Phone extensibility and certified Connect transfers do not remove the need for that identifier. A mailbox legal hold does not retain a partner’s compliance recording.
lessons.say: Screen pop needs E.164 and should write the Call-ID. Teams alone does not open the case.
lessons.fault: The pop shows the wrong person because the trunk prefix was left on.
lessons.listen: Pop the CRM from an E.164 number and store the Call-ID. Do not expect an ordinary Teams call to open Dynamics by itself.

lessons.title: AI agents beside the queue
lessons.why: A bot is a front door with a failure mode, not a headcount reduction you can assume.
body: Put the agent in front of a queue only when knowledge sources are grounded, the escape digit works, and unknown intent reaches a human. Generative orchestration is less predictable than classic topics. Evaluate prompt changes before they are on a public number. Foundry is the evaluation place, not a second SBC.

Troubleshooting: if callers loop, the recognize step has no escape or the fallback topic is empty. If answers are confident and wrong, the source document is wrong. Never place this bot on the emergency route.
lessons.say: The agent has a tested escape and a staffed overflow. It is not the emergency route.
lessons.fault: The prompt says ‘say agent’ and the recognize step has no such intent.
lessons.listen: An AI agent needs grounded sources, a human escape, and a real queue behind it.

lessons.title: Integration maps
lessons.why: A goal implies a set of systems. Naming them prevents a tool from being asked to do a job it does not have.
body: Recording regulated calls implies a certified recorder, an application instance, a policy, the users in scope, and a Call-ID. A CRM pop implies E.164 and middleware. Staffing implies queue intervals and shrinkage. WAN survival implies Direct Routing and an SBA. A bad building implies CQD and the subnet map. A bot implies an escape and a queue.
The integration-map lab asks you to pick the goal and read that list. If your design’s list is shorter, the missing row is the future incident.

chart.title: Goals to systems
chart.note: Use the lab for the full list.

lessons.say: I start from the goal and list the systems, including the identifier.
lessons.fault: The design’s list is shorter than the goal requires.
lessons.listen: For each goal, name the systems and the identifier. A shorter list is a future incident.

lessons.title: Cross-platform bridges
lessons.why: CUCM, Webex, UCCE, Genesys, and Amazon Connect all show up next to Teams. The bridge is an SBC and a rule, not a slogan.
body: The bridge is a certified SBC, often CUBE, with one normalization owner, a written number range, and a rollback that still has the old route. Identity is not shared automatically between CUCM and Entra. Presence is not a call route. Chat interop is not voice.

Genesys needs a named Connect, Extend, or Unify certification. Amazon Connect needs a drawn SIP path. UCCE agents stay put until the contact-center migration is its own project. Tromboning during dual-running is expected and should not become the steady state.
lessons.say: A cross-platform voice bridge is an SBC, one normalizer, written ranges, and a rollback.
lessons.fault: Both systems transform numbers, or the old trunk is deleted the same night.
lessons.listen: Bridge other platforms with a certified SBC, one place that normalizes, and a rollback you still have.

lessons.title: Future-integration hooks
lessons.why: A seam you name now is cheap. A rewrite after go-live is not. These hooks use products that exist today.
body: Leave these seams: store the Call-ID on the CRM timeline, assign the recording policy in the same change as the number, let overflow become a bot without a new public number, keep one subnet list, route by SBC FQDN rather than a copied proxy IP, make queue intervals exportable to WFM, test the human escape, and monitor certificate expiry.
None of these require an unannounced feature. A design that depends on a rumor is not a hook. It is a risk. The lab lists the failure you get if you skip each seam.

chart.title: Hooks
chart.note: Eight seams. The lab explains the miss.

lessons.say: I can name the seams I am leaving, and the failure if I skip one. I am not promising an unannounced product.
lessons.fault: The number goes live and the regulated users are not in a recording policy.
lessons.listen: Leave seams you can build today: Call-ID, recording policy, overflow, one subnet list, certificate dates. Do not design on a rumor.

lessons.title: Configuring an ecosystem change
lessons.why: A voice change that ignores the sisters will pass a test call and fail the business.
body: Write the change as a list: tenant, license, route, emergency subnet, recording policy, queue or workstream, CRM field, and the rollback. Do the lab version first. Read effective policy after each grant. Acquire resource-account licenses even when the price is zero.
Include the certificate expiry and the holiday calendar if the change touches an attendant. Include shrinkage if the change adds a queue. A test call by itself is not an ecosystem test.
lessons.say: My change list names the sisters, not only the SBC.
lessons.fault: The pilot is declared production because one test call worked.
lessons.listen: Configure an ecosystem change as a list: route, location, recorder, CRM, and rollback. A single test call is not enough.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting across a vendor boundary
lessons.why: The fault is usually on one side of a boundary. The argument is usually on both.
body: Name the boundary: Teams and SBC, SBC and carrier, Teams and recorder, queue and WFM, number and CRM. Collect the join key on both sides before anyone changes anything. Call-ID for SIP. E.164 for the CRM. Interval timestamp for WFM. Subnet for E911 and CQD.

One change, on the side the evidence names. Vendor-first if it is the SBC. Partner-first if it is the recorder. Do not restart a carrier trunk because a Copilot answer was wrong. Write the pack down so next month does not start from zero.

chart.title: Join keys
chart.note: Use the key that matches the boundary.

lessons.say: I name the boundary and the join key before I ask a vendor to change anything.
lessons.fault: Three vendors change three boxes because nobody wrote down the Call-ID.
lessons.listen: Across vendors, name the boundary and match the identifier. Then change one thing.
